Morning Newsletter Briefing (2026-09-02):
Good morning. It is 09:13 ET and markets are waking up to a rare triple driver: a global bond rout, a fresh geopolitical oil spike, and an AI earnings revival that is keeping the bulls from completely giving up. The S&P 500 enters midweek near 7,631, but the setup feels binary—either the 10-year stabilizes below 4.85% and tonight's AI earnings (Broadcom, Snowflake, HPE) confirm Dell's enthusiasm, or yields and crude break higher and force a defensive repositioning across equities and credit.

### 🌐 The Macro & Cross-Asset Narrative

Global rates are repricing at a generational speed. Bloomberg's G7 aggregate government-bond yield index hit its highest level since 2000 on Tuesday, led by a renewed U.S. Treasury selloff. The 10-year Treasury yield closed near 4.796% after rising another 4 bps—its highest since January 2025. Official FRED data show the 10-year at 4.75% (Aug. 31) and the 2-year at 4.34%, leaving the 10s-2s curve spread near +0.40%—still positive, but narrow enough to keep the entire policy-error debate very much alive.

The full bond map is lit up: 30-year UK gilts reached their highest yield since 1998; Japan's 10-year broke above 3% for the first time since 1996; Germany's 10-year yield touched 3.35%, the highest in over a decade; France's 10-year is hovering near 2008 levels. The bond market is not just repricing the Fed—it is repricing global debt sustainability and term premium.

Meanwhile, the effective federal funds rate is 3.63% (FRED, Aug. 1), after an easing cycle. Yet markets now price roughly 70% odds of a September rate hike. That is an extraordinary reversal, and the driver is clear: oil. The U.S.-Iran confrontation resumed near the Strait of Hormuz, sending Brent crude from $90 to $95 in a matter of days. Wednesday has Brent bid again at $95.52, with WTI at $90.76. Sticky inflation is reflected in the latest FRED index prints—headline CPI at 332.81, core CPI at 336.79, and PCEPI at 131.66—all pointing to a hot energy price shock arriving with none of last year's disinflation offset.

In cross-asset terms, the dollar is holding a firm bid, while the Sprott Physical Gold Trust fell 3.08% on Tuesday because real yields are rising. Gold is no longer the hedge; it is the victim of the rates shock. Bitcoin slid to $77,257 (-2.08%) and remains a high-beta risk asset, not an inflation hedge. The high-yield market is still relaxed—ICE BofA High Yield OAS is 2.63%—telling you credit has not broken. But if oil reaches $100 and the 10-year pushes toward 5%, credit will be the next shoe to drop.

### 🔬 Sector & Earnings Spotlight

Somewhere inside this broad risk-off tape, AI is still running its own bull market. Dell's print after Tuesday's close was exactly the kind of proof risk appetite needed. Revenue hit $47 billion, up 58% year over year; non-GAAP operating income was $5.9 billion, up 160%; and EPS grew more than 200%. Management raised fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to $192 billion, a $25 billion increase over its prior outlook and roughly $18 billion above the Street. Dell also cited record AI server orders and a rapidly expanding backlog tied to hyperscalers, neoclouds, and sovereign AI programs. Shares fell 6.94% in the regular session to $424.36, but are up about 8.5% premarket toward $460.

The AI borrowing boom is also broadening. Zero-coupon convertible issuance reached roughly $80 billion in 2026—about 43% of total convertible issuance and the largest annual figure since 1995. AI-related supply chains account for roughly 60% of these deals. The latest eyebrow-raiser is Nvidia investing $3.5 billion of a $3.9 billion zero-coupon convertible issued by MediaTek, with Alphabet also participating. Companies are monetizing their high equity valuations to finance AI capex without paying cash coupons—an aggressive but telling reflection of investor enthusiasm.

Tonight, the earnings spotlight shifts to Broadcom, Snowflake, and HPE. The bar is high. MongoDB fell 13.94% after hours despite beating top- and bottom-line estimates—EPS of $1.90 versus $1.61 expected, revenue of $772 million versus $734 million expected. The message is clear: bad news is punished, but merely good news is not enough anymore. Palo Alto Networks also beat and saw shares slip as management warned that AI could be weaponized by attackers. Elsewhere, GoPro surged 40% after Starman Optical agreed to acquire the company for $285 million in cash, with plans to move into defense and robotics. The sector story is bifurcation: AI infrastructure and networking are being bid up, while high-multiple software without an AI catalyst is being sold on any strength.

### 📈 Market Internals, Sentiment & Flows

The index tape is unambiguously risk-off after three straight losing sessions: S&P 500 -0.71% at 7,631.54, Nasdaq -1.03% at 26,099.77, and Dow -0.79% at 52,767.59. Breadth is negative, and futures are flat to slightly lower premarket. Volatility is climbing again, with the VIX waking up from its summer slumber, though the drawdown remains orderly at roughly 3% from the highs. There is no capitulation yet.

Importantly, credit is not confirming the equity stress. The ICE BofA US High Yield OAS is just 2.63%, and M2 sits at $23.2 trillion, so systemic liquidity is still abundant. What we are seeing is an inflation-driven rates shock rather than a credit event. That is why the flows are so odd: instead of fleeing risk entirely, institutional investors are piling into zero-coupon convertibles and AI equities. Convertible markets are effectively trading cash interest coupons for future equity optionality. If AI stocks keep rallying, the convertibles will be quickly converted into equity and dilute future shares; if AI stocks stall, those converts become expensive convexity bets that disappoint. For now, this dynamic is providing a powerful tailwind to the very names issuing the bonds.

Options sentiment is also likely to be defensive into tonight's earnings cluster. The S&P 500's 7,600 area has become the key gamma zone. A decisive close below 7,550 will likely trigger dealer hedging and accelerate downside. A close above 7,700, on the other hand, would squeeze short-term bears and set up a retest of 7,750–7,800. The next twenty-four hours will likely reset several weeks of positioning.

**Trade 1: SPX 7,600–7,700 inflection zone**

- Catalyst: Dell's after-hours beat, tonight's AVGO/SNOW/HPE reports, and the bond/oil reaction.
- Bull scenario: If the 10-year stabilizes below 4.85% and Brent fades below $93, the S&P can reclaim 7,700. A daily close above 7,700 is the long trigger, targeting 7,750–7,800, with a stop near 7,610.

- Invalidation: A quick de-escalation between Washington and Tehran would reverse the energy bid and could snap yields lower, giving equities an immediate bid.

- Catalyst: Renewed U.S.-Iran strikes and the credible threat of Strait of Hormuz disruption.
- Entry: A pullback into the $93.50–$94.50 zone offers a defined risk entry. Stop below $91.50, first target $99–$100.

- Invalidation: Confirmed U.S.-Iran negotiations, release of strategic reserves, or a sharp jump in OPEC spare capacity headlines.

**Trade 3: AI earnings after the bell—let the market tell you**

- Catalyst: Broadcom, Snowflake, and HPE report after the close.
- Best approach: Avoid guessing into the prints. Wait for the first 30 minutes of trading Thursday. If AVGO rallies and holds gains with volume, it confirms the AI trade remains healthy. If it fades below the pre-market printed levels, use that as a tactical signal to trim AI exposure.
- Key monitor: Dell's post-earnings strength may be the baseline for tonight's AI reporters. Any company that cannot rally on a beat will be seen as a disappointment—that is the current regime.

### 🗓️ The Catalyst Radar & Key Levels

The macro calendar is quiet today, which means oil headlines and earnings will drive the tape. Thursday brings weekly jobless claims, and Friday delivers the September jobs report—one of the last key data prints before the Fed's decision. August CPI follows the jobs report and will be the next inflation flashpoint. Given the market is now pricing ~70% odds of a September hike, the labor market and inflation data have amplified significance.

Earnings after the close today:

- Broadcom (AVGO)
- Snowflake (SNOW)
- HPE (HPE)

Key technical levels to watch:

- Nasdaq Composite: 26,099.77 current; support 25,800; resistance 26,500.

Stay small into the earnings cluster, respect the 10-year as the boss, and let tonight's AI prints tell you whether Dell is the exception or the new rule.

### 🌐 The Macro & Cross-Asset Narrative

Wall Street walked into Thursday’s open with a temporary truce: risk assets caught a bid on Wednesday, ending a three-session losing streak, but the underlying fault lines — an oil shock, a global bond rout, and an increasingly twitchy AI trade — have not gone anywhere.

Equities are now grinding sideways. The **S&P 500** settled at **7,666.60** (+0.46%), the **Nasdaq** added **0.45%** to **26,217.83**, and the **Dow** gained **0.56%** to **53,061.95**. Thursday pre-market futures offered little follow-through: S&P futures were up roughly **0.24%** and Nasdaq futures only **0.11%**, suggesting buyers lack conviction after two straight months of turbulence.

**Oil is the gravity point.** Brent crude futures touched the mid-$90s in the cash session and are now hovering near **$97**, up from the low-$80s a month ago. More troubling, diesel fuel futures have set fresh all-time highs — a direct pass-through to shipping costs, food prices, and consumer inflation expectations. The catalyst is the conflict around the **Strait of Hormuz**, where attacks on commercial vessels have not just disrupted energy flows but effectively removed tanker capacity from the global shipping pool. For context, shipping equities have seen their strongest rally in decades as freight rates explode. But analysts are quick to warn that the premium could unwind violently if there is any sign of de-escalation or a renewed Russia-Ukraine peace track.

Meanwhile, fixed income is telling an even more layered story. The **10-year Treasury constant maturity yield** stood at **4.79%**, a level not seen in nearly three years. The **2-year Treasury** yield is at **4.39%**, and the 10Y-2Y spread is a positive **~40 bps**, meaning the yield curve is no longer inverted — but for the wrong reasons. This is not an aggressive Fed easing signal; it is a term premium shock driven by inflation risk, deficit funding pressure, and geopolitical uncertainty. Official FRED data put the effective federal funds rate at **3.63%**, which means long-duration investors are demanding a hefty compensation for holding US debt. The **ICE BofA US High Yield Index OAS** has widened modestly to **2.65%**, but credit markets have yet to signal genuine distress.

This is not just a US story. The UK’s 10-year gilt hit its highest level since 2008, Germany’s 10-year bund reached a 2011 high, and Japanese government bond yields touched their highest level since 1996. Global bond markets appear to be pricing in a “higher-rate era,” partly because fiscal deficits remain enormous and partly because an oil-driven inflation impulse is forcing central banks to keep restrictive policies for longer. The **yen was rallying** overnight, and with the offshore risk backdrop still tense, the FX space is starting to look far less one-dimensional.

It was ever thus in September: equities, oil, rates, and geopolitical headlines are now intertwined. The core macro dynamic remains straightforward: **If oil prices hold above $95 and long yields move to 5%, equities will struggle to make upward progress. If Friday’s jobs data runs soft and oil pulls back, the market can breathe again.** The next 48 hours will set the tone.

### 🔬 Sector & Earnings Spotlight

The earnings tape overnight delivered one of the most striking AI divergences in months: **Broadcom** beat, warned, and fell; **Snowflake** beat, accelerated, and exploded higher.

#### Broadcom’s “Good Miss”
**Broadcom** reported fiscal Q3 revenue of **$29.59 billion**, up **86% year over year** — comfortably above expectations. Adjusted EPS also beat, and AI semiconductor revenue topped estimates, reinforcing the view that custom AI accelerators remain in hot demand. Yet shares fell about **5%** in after-hours trading after the company issued Q4 guidance below consensus. The market’s reflex reaction is a reminder that Big Tech is no longer rewarded purely for beating the past; guidance is the currency that matters. Management’s framing that revenue could **double in 2027 and 2028** helped soften the blow for longer-term holders, but the initial read-through is: the AI boom is intact, just not linear.

#### Snowflake’s Acceleration
**Snowflake** was the star of the evening. The data-cloud company posted adjusted EPS of **$0.62** on revenue of **$1.55 billion**, while product revenue grew **37% year over year**. The third consecutive acceleration in product growth convinced investors that Snowflake has finally found its growth groove after years of digestion. Full-year guidance was ratcheted higher, and shares jumped roughly **23% after hours**, hitting a fresh 52-week high early Thursday. This earnings print could become a crucial test for high-multiple software names into year-end.

#### The AI/Robotaxi Cross-Currents
The autonomous driving race also moved in several directions overnight. **Uber** is cutting about **10%** of its global workforce (~3,300 employees) in a drive to strip management layers and refocus on core mobility and delivery — a structural efficiency shift visible across the entire gig-economy complex. Still, Uber was up **~1.5% pre-market** after **Delivery Hero’s board recommended shareholders accept Uber’s $14.8 billion takeover offer**, and after Uber and Wayve launched passenger robotaxi trials in London. Meanwhile, **Waymo** is reportedly in final-stage talks to raise more than **$3 billion** in its first-ever external debt, tapping Blackstone and Pimco as it expands to San Diego, Denver, and Tampa. Today, all eyes are on **Tesla’s Cybercab launch event in Austin**, where roughly 50 robotaxis are already in operation. Morgan Stanley says the Street will need to see real scale, not just a handful of vehicles, to get excited. The convergence is finally happening — but the competitive landscape is more crowded than ever.

#### Google Wins / MapQuest Does Not
In a decision that surprised few legal watchers but still matters profoundly, **US District Judge Leonie Brinkema refused to force Google to divest its ad-tech business**, despite prior findings that the ad stack was an illegal monopoly. The court did accept several behavioral remedies intended to loosen Google’s control over publisher ad tools, but the headline is clear: the antitrust break-up wave is not materializing as feared. It is a huge overhang removal for **Alphabet**, and by extension, mega-cap technology.

In a far quirkier story, **MapQuest** shot to No. 1 in the App Store charts after refusing to rename Lake Ontario, sending parent **System1** stock up **~6%**. Pure 2026 energy.

Elsewhere in the tape, **shipping and tanker stocks** remain the strongest momentum pocket. **Agricultural commodities** are also in focus, with the Invesco DB Agricultural Fund up **7.4% in three months** — a byproduct of rising fertilizer and petroleum input costs. Food inflation is becoming a serious macro concern, and the upcoming El Niño cycle threatens even more upward pressure.

### 📈 Market Internals, Sentiment & Flows

Wednesday’s bounce was broad but not explosive. All three major indices gained about half a percent, and **Nvidia** added **3.2%**, helping to lead the rebound. Still, the internals show unease: the S&P 500 is essentially round-tripping in a tight range, and pre-market futures are fading, suggesting the bulge-bracket bid is absent.

Instrument-wise, the bond market is the dominant macro force. With 10-year Treasury yields near multi-year highs, equity valuations are being repriced at a discount rate that many investors feel is unwarranted. The **10-year yield at 4.79%** is particularly damaging to high-duration growth stocks, and the fact that the **2-year yield at 4.39%** remains closer to the effective funds rate means the current steepening is not a vote of confidence in rate cuts but a warning about long-term inflation and deficits.

Sentiment is defensive without being panicked. The high-yield OAS at **2.65%** still reflects broad risk appetite, and **M2 money supply** remains at a healthy **$23.2 trillion**, suggesting liquidity is not the binding constraint. But **Barclays** opened September with a clear note: take risk off the table. September is historically the worst month for equities, and with oil pushing $100, wage data still inconsistent, and central banks on hold, the asymmetry has shifted.

Options desks are bracing for a choppy two-way tape. Analysts such as Michael Kramer are flagging the possibility of an unwind, while precious metals strategists see silver targeting **$68.89** weekly mean levels above VC PMI support. The takeaway: this is not a market for complacent bulls or aggressive bears; it is a market for defined risks and tactical positioning.

### 💡 Trade Ideas & Scenarios to Watch

**1. Energy & Transportation Complexity — Buy the Pullback, Respect the Break**
The shipping/tanker trade has already enjoyed a massive run, so chasing extended names at the open is dangerous. Instead, look for a tactical long in crude or an energy-equity basket if **Brent pulls back into the $93-$94 zone** while holding above **$91**. The catalyst is acute supply disruption in Hormuz; the trigger is a bullish petroleum inventory print or an extended closure of the strait. Resistance lies at the psychological **$100** barrier, with support at **$90**. If a credible de-escalation headline hits, positions should be cut, with invalidation on a close below **$90**.

**2. Snowflake — Growth Acceleration But Rich Entry**
**Snowflake** has gapped to a 52-week high. The fundamental story — revenue acceleration, expanding product attach, and raised guidance — is exactly what the market wants. The setup: buy a pullback toward the **$350-360** post-gap support zone, or wait for a fresh high-volume breakout above the first resistance near **$400**. Invalidation is a close below **$320**, which would signal the gap has been completely filled and momentum is fading. Earnings momentum can carry stocks for weeks, but the AI tape is also prone to violent repricing when yields climb.

**3. Rate Steepener via the Back End**
If inflation data continues to impress, 10-year yields could drift above **4.85%** and eventually approach the psychological **5%** ceiling. The entry: buy small duration shorts (or a put spread on TLT) on a confirmed break of the **4.80%** level. Support is at **4.60%** if oil reverses. The invalidation is a soft jobs report that fuels aggressive rate-cut pricing, sending yields sharply lower.

**Bull Scenario (Probability ~40%)**
Oil stalls below $100. Friday’s payrolls are soft enough to support rate-cut hopes but not so weak as to signal recession. The S&P 500 reclaims **7,700** and rotates back into mega-cap tech, led by a stabilised Broadcom and a gapped-up Snowflake. High-yield spreads stay contained, and the US 10-year stays below **4.85%**. In that world, the September dip is a buying opportunity, and the equity index can attempt a new all-time high into month-end.

**Bear Scenario (Probability ~35%)**
Oil breaks above $100, diesel prices push inflation expectations higher, and the 10-year yield crosses **5%**. Equities lose their three-day-old foothold, with the S&P 500 sliding back through **7,600** — the key consolidation floor. High-yield spreads would likely widen sharply from **2.65%** to over **3%**, triggering a broader risk-off move in credit and crypto. Watch **Bitcoin** at $77k: a breakdown below **$75k** would signal that tightening financial conditions are overwhelming the liquidity narrative.

**Muddle-Through Scenario (Probability ~25%)**
Oil remains volatile but rangebound; yields stay locked in a 4.70%-4.85% band; Friday’s data offers no clear direction. This is the most dangerous environment for passive longs because equity indices will trade lower highs and lower lows while stock pickers feast. Sector rotation is king — favour energy, defense, and select AI infrastructure over consumer discretionary and long-duration software.

### 🗓️ The Catalyst Radar & Key Levels

**Today’s lineup:**
- **Tesla Cybercab launch event in Austin** — earlier update; expect more autonomous vehicle headlines throughout the day.
- **Rolling Fed speeches**; commentary on oil-driven inflation will be parsed for hawkishness.
- **Ongoing Strait of Hormuz headlines** — any military or diplomatic shift will immediately move oil, shipping, and tanks.

**Tomorrow and next week:**
- **September 4 (Friday) — US Nonfarm Payrolls (August)** is the marquee event for this shortened trading week. The unemployment rate currently sits at **4.10%**, and Friday’s wages + participation data will guide the Fed’s path. Weak employment could revive rate-cut bets and drag yields lower, while hot wages risk pushing the 10-year toward the **5%** threshold.
- **Jobless Claims** and **ISM Services PMI** will be monitored before the headline report.
- Watch for **august CPI and PCE prints** later in the month; the latest CPI index registered **332.81**, with core at **336.79**, and the PCE price index at **131.66** — elevated enough to make any fresh energy shock uncomfortable.

**Key technical levels to track:**
- **S&P 500:** support at **7,590-7,600**, resistance at **7,680-7,700**. Wednesday’s close of **7,666.60** sits just under the first springboard level.
- **Nasdaq:** support at **25,900**, resistance at **26,500**.
- **US 10-year yield:** pivot at **4.79%**; a break of **4.85%** opens a path to **5.00%**; a break below **4.60%** relieves equity pressure.
- **WTI/Brent:** psychological resistance at barrel pricing of **$100** Brent; bullish continuation through the gasoline and diesel contract spreads.
- **Bitcoin:** current $77k level remains a sentiment barometer. A break below $75k would coincide with weakness in high-beta risk assets.

**Bottom line:** September is off to a tense start. The Fed may be done hiking at **3.63%** effective, but the bond market is doing the tightening itself, and oil is writing the daily narrative. Today’s new equilibrium will hinge on whether the AI earnings complex can absorb a higher discount rate, and whether jobs data next week finally gives the macro picture clarity. Until then, play tight defence, size positions down, and keep your catalysts on speed dial.

**Friday, September 4, 2026 — 09:13 ET**

The August jobs report has landed, and it was stronger than expected. Nonfarm payrolls rose by 162,000 in August, well above the 53,000 Dow Jones consensus that was being cited ahead of the release. The immediate reaction is not a straight-line risk-on bid: S&P 500 futures are down roughly 0.2%, Dow futures are off 0.26%, and Nasdaq futures are hovering around flat as rates traders digest where the Fed goes next. This morning’s print wraps up a week that already had plenty of moving parts: Tesla’s Cybercab launch, Nvidia’s $13B Hugging Face acquisition, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra rollout, and one of the best risk-asset sessions in a month.

### 🌐 The Macro & Cross-Asset Narrative

The official FRED data frame the policy tension clearly. The federal funds effective rate printed 3.63% in August, meaning the market is debating whether the FOMC stays put or delivers another 25bp move later this month. In the Treasury market, the 10-year constant-maturity yield was 4.79% as of September 2 and closed around 4.76% Thursday after falling 3bps. The 2-year sits near 4.39%, leaving the 10-year/2-year spread at roughly +43bps. That is a positive, re-steepened curve — a far cry from the deeply inverted curve of 2023-2024, and a sign that duration risk is back at the center of the macro conversation.

Thursday’s cash session set a constructive backdrop. The S&P 500 finished at **7,747.71**, up **+1.06%**. The Dow climbed **+1.18%** to **53,686.11** — gaining about 624 points for its best day in a month — and the Nasdaq rallied **+1.40%** to **26,584.06**. The upside came after Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he is inclined to support holding rates steady at the September meeting. According to the eToro briefing, market-implied September rate-hike odds dropped from roughly 65% to 54% after Waller’s comments, directly challenging the more hawkish Jackson Hole posture associated with Fed leadership under Kevin Warsh.

Today’s 162K NFP print, however, pours cold water on the idea that the Fed can simply wait. The strong headline is not just about aggregate hiring; it complicates the inflation narrative. The CPI data for July show the all-items index at **332.81**, core CPI at **336.79**, and the PCE headline price index at **131.66**. Waller’s argument is that core PCE rose just 0.2% in July and that three months of progress argue for patience. The hotter jobs number gives the hawkish side a counter: the economy can withstand tightening, and labor-market resilience reduces the urgency to avoid a hike if inflation risks persist.

Cross-asset behavior also has a new structural twist. The old correlation regime — stocks and Treasury yields rising together on growth optimism — has broken down. As Axios Markets notes, the S&P 500’s correlation with the 10-year Treasury yield has turned increasingly negative. Rising yields used to be a vote of confidence in nominal growth; now, when yields jump because of inflation scares, oil spikes, war premium, or Fed-policy confusion, equities tend to fall. That regime shift matters for every risk-parity and multi-asset allocation decision.

In commodities, crude oil is slipping but still near six-week highs amid elevated Iran and Hormuz-Strait supply risks. Diesel has reportedly hit an all-time high, which is a potential cost-push inflation channel that the core PCE data do not fully capture. Gold remains on the move as real-rate uncertainty and central-bank demand continue to underpin the complex; silver’s cycle breakout is being tracked with upside targets at **$68.89** and **$70.95**. Bitcoin rallied **+5.46%** yesterday to **$81,605**, a reminder that crypto remains highly sensitive to liquidity and Fed expectations. In FX, the dollar is broadly firm but direction is two-way; analysts at Investing.com are flagging USD/JPY and the yen carry trade as one of the most important volatility triggers if global rate assumptions shift quickly.

### 🔬 Sector & Earnings Spotlight

Thursday’s breadth was unusually strong, and the premarket earnings headlines are bringing the knives out for consumer-discretionary names.

**Lululemon** is the biggest story. The athletic-apparel retailer cratered roughly 20% premarket after issuing a sharply weaker quarterly outlook. Management guided to earnings of **$0.93–$0.98 per share** on revenue of **$2.29B–$2.32B** — far below analyst estimates across both metrics. The stock had already been under pressure from softer North American demand, and this guide confirms that the premium-athleisure slowdown is not cyclical noise. If LULU opens south of **$120**, it opens a path toward the low **$110s**, and dip-buyers will be scarce until the chart shows a base.

Elsewhere in the consumer complex, Campbell’s fell 6.96% to **$22.13** after announcing a 13% workforce reduction, a distressed restructuring signal from a struggling packaged-food company. Docusign provided a useful counterweight in software: the company beat Q2 earnings and revenue expectations, raised the high end of its full-year revenue outlook, and materially increased its non-GAAP operating-margin forecast. Asana, by contrast, tumbled after Q3 guidance disappointed, illustrating that even tech earnings are becoming more discriminating.

In autos, Volkswagen is rallying after its board approved a radical restructuring plan, and Tesla is the other headline auto name. Tesla formally added the **Cybercab** to its robotaxi fleet, launching public rides in limited parts of Austin on Thursday. The matte-gold, steering-wheel-free, pedal-less two-seater has no manual controls, which is why federal regulators are evaluating the rollout. CEO Elon Musk reiterated the cost angle — roughly **20–40 cents per mile** — but the path to scale remains the key debate. TSLA rose 5% Thursday but gave back 2.3% premarket, leaving the stock vulnerable to regulatory headlines.

The biggest strategic story of the week is in AI infrastructure: **Nvidia confirmed plans to acquire Hugging Face** for approximately **$13 billion**. Hugging Face is often described as the GitHub of AI — the central repository where open-source models, weights, and adaptations live. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang framed the deal as a bet on open-source AI ecosystems, sovereignty, security, and innovation. The financials are notable: Hugging Face reportedly rejected a $500M investment from Nvidia at a $7B valuation in January, only to approach Nvidia later after sustaining pressure from proprietary AI agents scraping its platform. Nvidia’s broader equity-investment portfolio now totals a stunning **$99B**, up $92B year-over-year, highlighting how the company is vertically integrating across model labs, cloud providers, and infrastructure.
